v.why: Pushing an already strong L2 penalty toward 1 forces weights near zero and causes underfitting, unlike the harmless or helpful step from mid values.
L2 acts on every layer so shrinkage compounds with depth and slows fitting within 243 epochs.
Tiny batches already supply implicit regularization and many update steps apply the decay often, so extra L2 mostly causes underfitting.
Narrow nets are capacity-limited so additional L2 pushes them into underfitting.
With a tiny learning rate training is step-limited, so fewer updates per epoch from larger batches leave the model undertrained.
Larger batches average out the gradient noise that a very high learning rate amplifies, stabilizing training.
Tiny batches combined with a very high learning rate give noisy, frequent large Adam steps that destabilize or diverge.
Strong L2 slows fitting and more update steps per epoch from smaller batches help compensate within a fixed epoch budget.
Extra layers need more optimization progress, which a tiny learning rate cannot deliver in 243 epochs.
Deeper stacks are more prone to divergence and dead ReLUs at very large learning rates, so adding a layer hurts more.
Strong L2 applied to more layers compounds shrinkage and underfits.
Very narrow nets are capacity-bottlenecked so widening gives large gains, whereas wide nets are saturated.
A single hidden layer relies on width for all its capacity, so widening substitutes for missing depth.
Wide layers make each Adam step change outputs much more, so a very high learning rate becomes unstable.
At learning rates around 1e-5 to 1e-4 the net is badly undertrained in 243 epochs, so raising it gives a large gain.
Raising an already huge learning rate toward 1 causes divergence and collapse to near-chance accuracy.
Reducing a divergent-scale learning rate restores stable training and large accuracy gains.
Large batches have low gradient noise and few steps per epoch, so they tolerate and need a larger learning rate.
With tiny batches updates are already numerous and noisy, so a higher learning rate pushes training into instability.
Very wide nets are already fast learners and more sensitive to step size, so raising the learning rate overshoots sooner.
